conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor today. You came in with weakness and lightheadedness after a couple days of diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two days ago I started having watery, foul-smelling bowel movements—about five that night. No blood. Then yesterday morning I vomited clear mucus, and later I felt so weak and dizzy, like the room was spinning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been managing your Addison’s disease for years. Did you think this might be an adrenal crisis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wasn’t sure. I’ve learned to recognize the signs—fatigue, dizziness, salt craving. I’ve been drinking broth and extra fluids. I called my endocrinologist yesterday, and she told me to take an extra Florinef tablet because my potassium was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was a good call. In the ER, your heart rate was high—113—and your blood pressure dropped a bit when you stood up, which suggests you were a little dehydrated. We started you on IV fluids and gave you your morning prednisone and thyroid medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried. With Addison’s, even a small illness can turn serious. I didn’t want to take chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing coming in. We checked your labs, and your sodium was a bit low, potassium slightly high—consistent with mild adrenal insufficiency during illness. But no fever, and your chest X-ray was clear. No signs of infection or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just the stomach bug? I’ve been renovating at home—no kitchen, eating off a table. Maybe something got contaminated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very possible. Symptoms point to a viral infection, maybe norovirus. Diarrhea has stopped, and you haven’t vomited since arriving. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. You’ve received 2 liters of IV fluids so far. Your heart rate has come down to 99, and blood pressure is stable at 100/60. We’re giving you another liter to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Still tired, but the dizziness is less when I sit up. What about my back pain? It’s been bothering me—the rhomboid area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. You got IV Dilaudid in the ER for it, but we’d prefer to avoid heavy opioids. We can give you oral oxycodone if needed, but let’s try to manage it conservatively now that you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your electrolytes are improving. Sodium and potassium are normalizing. We’re stopping the IV fluids after this bag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you this afternoon. Your endocrinologist agreed: take double your usual prednisone dose today and tomorrow—so 15 mg total—then go back to 7.5 mg. You already took an extra Florinef yesterday, so resume your regular dose now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—Synthroid, Nexium, Fosamax—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll send you home with instructions to check your electrolytes in a few days at the lab on Level 7. The results will go to your PCP and endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing well—no dizziness, eating normally, and your back pain is manageable. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much safer knowing my levels are back on track. I’ll rest at home and keep an eye on things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call your doctor if dizziness returns or you can’t keep fluids down. Otherwise, follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge order is in. You’ll be leaving within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll make sure to take that double dose of prednisone today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we switched you from pantoprazole back to your usual Nexium. Everything else is as before, except no oxycodone refill. Use ibuprofen or clonazepam if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’ll stick to my regular routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your discharge instructions and medications. You’re cleared to go home when ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re all set to leave. Remember to take your double dose of prednisone today and tomorrow, and get those labs done.
